lesson_scope: Calculation and comparison of kinetic energy changes (1/2 mv^2 - 1/2 mu^2) and gravitational potential energy changes (mgh) for a single particle or rigid body in vertical motion and along inclined planes; application of the work-energy theorem (Net work = Delta E_k) and energy conservation (Work by driving force = Delta E_k + Delta E_p + Work against resistance); determination of resistive forces and deceleration distances.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Direct calculation of kinetic energy

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Direct calculation of kinetic energy

hints: Use the standard formula for kinetic energy: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Substitute $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ and $v = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $E_k = 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 14^2 = 49\text{ J}$.

walkthrough.text:
State the kinetic energy definition:
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$
Where $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ and $v = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Evaluate the formula:
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}(0.5)(14^2) = \frac{1}{2}(0.5)(196) = 49\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify mass and velocity:
- Given mass and speed:
$$m = 0.5\text{ kg},\quad v = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Compute kinetic energy:
- Half of mass times speed squared:
$$E_k = 0.25 \times 196 = 49\text{ J}$$
The particle possesses $49\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with $m = 0.5$ and $v = 14$.
Obtains kinetic energy $E_k = 49\text{ J}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 2: Kinetic energy change of an accelerating car

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 2: Kinetic energy change of an accelerating car

hints: The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$.

walkthrough.text:
State the formula for change in kinetic energy:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$$
With $m = 1200\text{ kg}$, $u = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $v = 22\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate the numerical increase:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}(1200)(22^2 - 10^2) = 600(484 - 100) = 600(384) = 230400\text{ J} \quad (230.4\text{ kJ})$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Set up the difference of squared speeds:
- Initial and final speeds squared:
$$u^2 = 100,\quad v^2 = 484 \implies v^2 - u^2 = 384\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$$

Compute kinetic energy gain:
- Multiply by half the mass:
$$\Delta E_k = 600 \times 384 = 230400\text{ J} = 230.4\text{ kJ}$$
The car gains $230.4\text{ kJ}$ of kinetic energy.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$ with $m = 1200$, $u = 10$, and $v = 22$.
Obtains increase in kinetic energy $\Delta E_k = 230400\text{ J}$ (or $230.4\text{ kJ}$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Falling body with air resistance using work-energy

hints: Compare the potential energy lost with the kinetic energy gained: $W_{\text{air}} = mgh - \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the potential energy lost and kinetic energy gained:
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = (0.4)(10)(15) = 60\text{ J}$$
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.4)(16^2) = 51.2\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy theorem to find work done against air resistance:
$$W_{\text{air}} = \Delta E_p - \Delta E_k = 60 - 51.2 = 8.8\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compare energy input and output:
- Potential energy released: $60\text{ J}$
- Kinetic energy acquired: $51.2\text{ J}$:
$$60 - 51.2 = 8.8\text{ J}$$

Deduce work done against air resistance:
- The missing energy was dissipated to the air:
$$W_{\text{air}} = 8.8\text{ J}$$
Air resistance absorbs $8.8\text{ J}$ of energy.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the kinetic energy at projection:
$$E_{k0} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(5)(10^2) = 250\text{ J}$$

Equate kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy at instantaneous rest ($v = 0$):
$$mgh = E_{k0} \implies (5)(10)h = 250$$
$$50h = 250 \implies h = 5\text{ m}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find initial energy:
- The block starts with pure kinetic energy:
$$E_{k0} = 2.5 \times 100 = 250\text{ J}$$

Apply conservation of mechanical energy:
- With no friction, all kinetic energy transforms into potential energy:
$$50h = 250 \implies h = 5\text{ m}$$
The block climbs to a vertical height of $5\text{ m}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates initial KE $\frac{1}{2}(5)(10^2) = 250\text{ J}$ and equates to $mgh = (5)(10)h$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 2: Block projected up a smooth inclined plane

hints: Use trigonometry along the incline: $d = \frac{h}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{5}{0.5} = 10\text{ m}$.
Halfway up the plane at height $h' = 2.5\text{ m}$, apply conservation of mechanical energy: $\frac{1}{2}(5)v^2 + 5(10)(2.5) = 250 \implies v = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate distance along the line of greatest slope:
$$d = \frac{h}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{5}{0.5} = 10\text{ m}$$

Set up the energy conservation equation at halfway distance ($s = 5\text{ m}$, height $h' = 5\sin 30^\circ = 2.5\text{ m}$):
$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh' = E_{k0}$$
$$\frac{1}{2}(5)v^2 + (5)(10)(2.5) = 250$$
$$2.5v^2 + 125 = 250 \implies 2.5v^2 = 125$$
$$v^2 = 50 \implies v = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07106\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 7.07\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Determine slope distance:
- Using the incline angle of $30^\circ$:
$$d = \frac{5}{\sin 30^\circ} = 10\text{ m}$$
The block travels $10\text{ m}$ up the plane.

Calculate speed halfway up:
- At $5\text{ m}$ along the slope, half the potential energy is gained ($125\text{ J}$), leaving half the kinetic energy ($125\text{ J}$):
$$2.5 v^2 = 125 \implies v^2 = 50$$
$$v = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
The speed halfway up is $7.07\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates distance along plane $d = \frac{h}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{5}{0.5} = 10\text{ m}$.
Applies energy conservation at halfway height $h' = 2.5\text{ m}$: $\frac{1}{2}(5)v^2 + (5)(10)(2.5) = 250$ (or applies $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$).
Obtains distance along plane $d = 10\text{ m}$ and speed $v = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 3: Car accelerating up an incline against resistance

hints: Work done by the engine supplies both mechanical energy changes and covers resistance: $W_{\text{engine}} = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p + W_{\text{resist}}$.
Subtract total mechanical energy increase from engine work: $W_{\text{resist}} = 340000 - (129600 + 162000) = 48400\text{ J}$.
Divide work done against resistance by the distance travelled along the slope: $F_{\text{resist}} = \frac{48400}{150} \approx 323\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the work-energy theorem for the motion:
$$W_{\text{engine}} = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p + W_{\text{resist}}$$
$$340000 = 129600 + 162000 + W_{\text{resist}}$$
$$340000 = 291600 + W_{\text{resist}}$$

Solve for the work done against resistance:
$$W_{\text{resist}} = 340000 - 291600 = 48400\text{ J} \quad (48.4\text{ kJ})$$

Calculate the average resistance force over the $150\text{ m}$ climb:
$$F_{\text{resist}} = \frac{W_{\text{resist}}}{d} = \frac{48400}{150} \approx 322.667\text{ N} \approx 323\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Form the work-energy balance:
- Engine input must balance mechanical energy gained plus resistance:
$$W_{\text{resist}} = 340000 - 291600 = 48400\text{ J}$$
$48.4\text{ kJ}$ is dissipated overcoming resistance.

Determine average resistance force:
- Spread over the $150\text{ m}$ climb:
$$F_{\text{resist}} = \frac{48400}{150} \approx 323\text{ N}$$
The average opposing force is $323\text{ N}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies work-energy principle: $W_{\text{engine}} = \Delta E_k + \Delta E_p + W_{\text{resist}}$.
Obtains work done against resistance $W_{\text{resist}} = 340000 - 129600 - 162000 = 48400\text{ J}$ (or $48.4\text{ kJ}$).
Calculates average resistance force $F_{\text{resist}} = \frac{48400}{150} \approx 323\text{ N}$ (or $322.7\text{ N}$).
